text: Many of these suggested practices are similar to or reflective of the preventative measures provided by many in the literature as outlined in Section 0 of this report [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 14]. 1. When rail cars are brought for service, they should be defueled immediately, preferably outdoors. If defueled indoors, the verification of leak-tightness of connections between the tank, valve, defueling tool, venting hose, and roof vent stack should be performed. 2. If a rail car is indoors, its TPRD vent stacks should be connected to outdoor venting in case they are activated. 3. Maintenance pits and ceiling areas should be unobstructed and well-ventilated to prevent accumulation of hydrogen to avoid flammable or asphyxiating conditions. For example, rails can be mounted on posts so that rail car pits are less enclosed and maintenance facility roofs can be designed to be blown off in case of an explosion. Ventilation requirements according to safety codes and standards such as NFPA 2 should be followed [29]. 4. Hot work procedures for hydrogen rail environments should be developed and followed closely. The atmosphere should be sampled using tools such as hydrogen sensors, katharometers, or UV/IR flame detectors before beginning hot work operations. Some requirements are provided in NFPA 2 in Chapter 4 and Annex K, such as ensuring that sparks are not introduced into any duct system potentially containing hydrogen [29]. 5. Anti-static and grounding devices should be utilized on systems during service. In addition, power sources and grounds should be rated for hazardous areas. 6. If air can be trapped in lines, they should be purged with inert gas before introduction of hydrogen. 7. Components such as tanks, lines, couplers, and gaskets should be designed, qualified, and material-compatible, so they are non-reactive and inhibit hydrogen diffusivity. These components should be installed properly, inspected regularly, maintained, and replaced when appropriate according to manufacturing or service protocols. 8. Workers should be regularly trained in start-up procedures, leak detection, pressure and voltage monitoring, inspection, component lifetime, installation, communication, documentation, and maintenance procedures to ensure they are performed consistently and properly. Supervision should be in place to observe and verify proper service work and perform random inspections, especially of installation and replacement of components. Additionally, further work can be devoted to experimentally or computationally examining the risks of release of large amounts of hydrogen from rail cars in a typical retrofitted maintenance facility. Additionally, since hydrogen may react with steel to induce crack growth especially at higher temperatures [30, 31], the interaction of hydrogen with specific types of steel components present on rail cars should be further studied to evaluate the potential for embrittlement, hazardous, or flammable conditions. 28 This page left blank 29 4. CONCLUSION This work identifies specific safety requirements and potential hazards of hydrogen rail maintenance environments. This study conducted a hazard and operability analysis, evaluating 1,092 potential scenarios to determine their consequences, causes, and severity.
